cues.t: Steve Yegge: It does kinda feel like I was invited to the wrong conference 'cause I'm not really a data guy.
For the last four years or so, I've been working on stuff that I love. OK?
And I'm gonna be talking about this more during the talk here.
I want you to remember this, though.
This is really important.
You don't want to put out mediocre work and you don't want to feel mediocre about what you're doing.
Surprisingly, we don't always do this.
So, I'll come back to it.
Right now, I work at Google.
And for the last four years at Google, I've been there for six and a half total, I've been working on compiler technology
because I have this passion around developer tools.
And I've been working on static program analysis.
So, when you take Google's source code and you treat it as data, you take all the world's Open Source code and you treat it as data,
it's actually not a very big data set.
It's, I don't know, a couple dozen terabytes, a couple hundred terabytes.
But it's pretty tiny compared to the big data sets at Google.
So, you know, and I've had scaling problems, but you know, I'm not really a data guy, per se.
But gosh, I work with people who do have data problems.
And I have to say just in passing, Google's an awesome place to work.
I went to work for Google, actually, specifically, because I think that Google is trying to change the world.
OK?
I mean, and they're serious about it.
And I kinda thought this when I went there six and a half years ago.
And after six and a half years, Google's the only ones trying to defend net neutrality when nobody else was.
Google trying to open up China.
I mean, that was pretty audacious, right?
They haven't always been successful in their goals, but man they have, they're really trying to change the world.
And they have big scaling problems.
Sometimes, it feels like it's their biggest problem.
It's funny 'cause scaling and we're all gonna be really focused on these details during this conference,
the technical details of making things scale.
But it's this periodic problem.
You need to scale 'cause you've got a problem to solve and then it's good enough for a while.
And you can focus on problem domains and then it becomes a problem again as you grow, just like software engineering scaling has been a problem on and off.
We're actually pretty good at it right now, whereas 10, 15 years ago, we were building software systems that we didn't understand.
So, we knew we needed to step back and get some new abstractions.
Anyway, before I was at, sorry, before I was at Google, I was at Amazon.com for six and a half years.
Another company that's trying to change the world.
Jeff Bezos has grand visions.
And it's another company with huge scaling problems.
Now, they are awesome, also.
It's a different flavor of awesome than Google.
They're pretty open about their work environment being very frugal, because their vision is to pass savings onto customers.
But I wasn't there for the work environment.
I wouldn't have stayed there six and a half years.
They have great people there and they have tremendous scaling problems.
Scaling really is often, too, their biggest problem.
Why?
Because they're fundamentally relational and transactional.
And I know what you're thinking.
[clear throat and fake spits] Right?
Nobody here like relational anymore.
But they have to make it scale.
OK?
I got one person to laugh. [laughter] But seriously, like, and they succeed at it, right?
And Google also has some transactional data.
Google uses MySQL for their ads system and it's really, really hard to scale, but you can make it happen.
And again, Amazon is a company that's not mercenary.
They're trying to make money and that's good 'cause money is the fuel for innovation.
But they're doing it with principle.
All right?
And the retail thing that Amazon did that was sort of like a means to an end, just like scaling is a means to an end, right?
Now they're doing cloud computing and Bezos has got big plans, right?
Just like Larry and Sergey.
So, what about the rest of us?
What are we doing right now?
What are we focused on?
Well, I wanna look at one of our sister industries here you're all real familiar with, Hollywood.
It's not exactly been a banner year for them, has it?
You might have noticed all the movies suck this year.
Twenty-eight sequels and comic book movies and why is this?
Well I mean, we know the reasons.
It's human nature.
It's corporate greed.
Companies being mercenary, taking advantage of consumer apathy.
If we keep paying to go see movies like Scream 4 and Hangover 2 and Transformers 17 and whatever,
then they'll keep making them.
Right?
And the same things are going on in the game industry.
The game industry, hundreds and hundreds of titles coming out.
I assume that some of you are like me and you like video games or you have kids who like video games.
You have friends who like video games.
And they're always complaining that there aren't any good games.
But there's so many good games, right?
There are talented people working on them.
Great animators, you know, great cinematographers and sound people.
But most of the games are pretty bad.
And again, it's 'cause people keep paying for them, so people keep making them.
Yeah, except for these guys.
Hollywood calls them "Auteurs." But what they really are is they're people who are making money,
but with principles.
Whether the principles are stretching you a little bit and making you think about philosophy and the nature of consciousness
while you're getting entertained, or they're bringing up social issues like trashing the world in WALL-E,
or putting some serious history into their game experience like Rockstar.
I mean, whatever it is that they're passionate about, it really bleeds through.
It shows through in their final product and making everyone else look bad.
And they're also showing that you can still make a ton of money with principle.
Jeff Bezos and Steve Jobs, they fall into this category.
I mean, anybody can have principle.
Bill Gates does today.
Right?
He's atoning for his past sins, right? [laughter] Did he have principle when he was at the helm at Microsoft?
No, obviously.
And now he knows well, he probably didn't need to be that way.
OK.
Hey, they promised me I could see my slides on this thing, but I can't.
So, I have no idea what's coming next.
Hell yeah.
This is what we're working on right now. [laughter] Is this principled?
I mean, seriously.
Who in here is not working on something that's kinda related to a social network?
OK. Whew!
Like five hands out of a thousand people in this room.
Seriously. OK?
Well, this is fun and this is also obviously making money.
You can make a buck with cat pictures, all right?
Social networks, I mean, they have a purpose.
You know, I mean, Facebook's purpose, I mean, the purpose is whatever they make easiest and so that's what people are gonna do over there.
And Facebook and Facebook clones, if anybody's making any of those, [laughter] is, they're really good at sharing cat pictures.
Now, they can have secondary benefits to humanity, like for example helping out with information flow in and out of the Middle East.
But that's not what they're designed for.
So, that's not what people are using them for.
And it winds up being crap, just like Hollywood's movies.
So, here's what happens over time.
As you get older, and that happened to me.
I don't know how it happened to me, right?
But I'm getting older.
You start getting interested in these broader problems than cat pictures.
I'm not saying that you don't, you're not interested in social anymore.
OK, obviously you wanna hang out with old people.
But you also get in interested in like, why they haven't cured heart disease yet, right?
And trust me; my heart's pounding up here, so I'm wondering like right now.
And as you gain wealth and you're not a total mercenary, then you start getting interested in charity and helping people who are needy.
And you start getting interested in politics and all these other hard problems.
And a lot of them, interestingly, are data mining problems.
Ooh, tie into our conference.
Well, the problem is by the time you're old, [chuckles] it's too late.
What you want is a time machine so you can go back and tell yourself, "Hey man, if you'd like, studied some math,
we could probably work on some of the hard problems like signal processing, right?" Voice recognition is an important problem because it's an accessibility thing.
It's putting blind people and deaf people in the same position we are.
Natural language processing.
Same thing.
Genes, viruses.
I mean, there's a bunch of problems out there that have the common characteristic that they're not just computing problems.
They're a little harder 'cause you gotta know a little bit of math, a little bit of statistics.
You don't have to be Hal Varian.
You just have to be fluent.
You have to be literate, right?
Well, here's an interesting problem that we could be working on if we were literate.
Have you guys thought about this project at all?
Human Genome Project, what is it?
The genome sequence they've got now is the compiled binary to the source code for the human body,
for life, the mechanics of life.
If we had the source code in our hands, that would be the cure for cancer right there.
That would be the cure for all the viruses, all of them, that would keep antibiotics ahead of bacteria.
Enumerable benefits.
We know this.
You could also hack things, like grow your own tattoo, right?
But it's meaningful.
It will be an inflection point in human history, OK?
And it's a data mining problem.
Now, I know a lot of you are already good at data mining.
I mean, there was like a dude sitting next to me at dinner last night named Jay, who was a freaking superhero.
He was a thousand times smarter than I am.
And I brought up this project and he says, "I'm not really a bioinformatics guy, but you know, ."
And he scribbles on the back of the napkin how you could set up this, you get a benevolent billionaire to set up a treatment system
in a Third World Country and start gathering data points and you could analyze the effectiveness of the treatments.
Because what we're trying to do would be compile binary, is reverse engineer the source code by data mining it against treatments.
And if you get that data set, then we're there, right?
He's like, "Yeah, but I'm not really a bioinformatics guy." What's he working on?
Cat pictures. [laughter] And he was like a closet superhero.
The dude sitting next to him was wearing a cape.
I'm not making this up.
All right.
He wasn't even trying to hide his superhero status.
You guys are superheroes.
And we're all working on, well, crap.
Most of us anyway.
Now, if we started focusing on these problems, I know it sounds crazy, but we would actually have a chance at solving them.
And if we just focus on scaling.
I mean, we're gonna scale up FarmVille.
It's gonna be FarmPlanet.
And I'm not saying FarmVille doesn't have value, I guess.
But, [laughter] yeah.
OK.
So what's needed here is pretty obvious.
It's a culture change.
We all need to be "Auteurs." Right?
We need to start buckling down now and preparing for getting old and getting interested in medicine and so on.
Start studying our math.
Start paying attention to data science.
It's not a specialty discipline anymore.
It's a generalist discipline.
It should be.
Even at Google, where there's a lot of people who know a lot about data mining, it's still the haves and the have nots, like me,
who don't know it.
Well, O'Reilly, amazingly enough, seems to be actually trying to change the world with this convention and with Strata.
Right?
I mean, they're actually saying, "Hey, gosh. Look.
Data.
Data mining.
Machine learning. Data analysis.
Math." Right?
Well, OK.
If we want a culture change, I've got a challenge.
I've got a challenge for O'Reilly and a challenge for us.
The challenge for O'Reilly is to publish a bunch of books on math for programmers, because O'Reilly's got a formula for making information accessible.
And well, let's go out on a limb.
Let's do physics.
Let's do bioinformatics.
Why not?
Let's give him two years to publish these things and then in that two-year period after they've published them all,
we will agree to buy them and read them and prepare ourselves to solve important problems five years from now.
Two years.
Whoa.
I meant two seconds.
They published them already.
Did you guys know this?
Female: Yes.
Steve Yegge: Yeah, well you did. OK.
So, look at this. OK?
Bioinformatics, Perl, Computer Skills, Mastering Perl for Bioinformatics.
An O'Reilly bioinformatics book.
A lot of these came out just in the last two or three years.
I didn't even know they existed, but something's going on here.
I'm reading between the lines.
I'm making some educated guesses, but I know that these books aren't selling.
So, why are they publishing them?
It's because Tim and his team are trying to change the world by affecting a culture change.
So, the ball is totally in our court.
And what's the ball doing?
Well, the ball's apparently doing iPad.
This is what's popular right now in O'Reilly's site.
I just took this screen shot yesterday.
Head First, that's kinda mathy.
The rest of it, PHP?
PHP. Come on. [laughter] I had to get a PHP joke in and I got one.
Captive audience.
All right.
So, but seriously.
Like, obviously O'Reilly is principled here.
'Cause if they were just trying to make a buck, they'd be throwing OSCON iPad, wouldn't they?
They would.
And they probably talked about it at length. [laughter] But no, they're doing OSCON Data.
So, why don't we just affect a culture change here?
I'm not saying, "Drop what we're doing right now." I mean, the world needs cat pictures.
But what if we all started studying data mining and so on.
And if you already know that stuff really well, then shame on you 'cause you're only one step away from solving hard problems,
important problems, world-changing problems, you've just gotta learn the domain knowledge.
You don't need to learn it overnight.
I do compiler stuff, static program analysis at Google.
I didn't know any of it four years ago.
Nothing.
But I had a compiler class in school.
And now, I'm not like Walter Bright or James Gosling, but I know compilers pretty well and I'm pretty proficient with them
and I can solve the problems that I need to solve.
Same thing goes for this, right?
So, here's the funny thing is I had a mid-life crisis instantly after writing and rehearsing this speech once.
I rehearsed it and I went, "Oh God.
I'm not following my own advice." So, I dragged my math books down from upstairs and put them on the table here.
And my wife and I are having study hour every day from now on.
Moreover, this is part of my mid-life crisis and this is gonna come as a real shock to my boss,
I had just signed up to work on a cat picture project. [laughter]
And I told everyone I was gonna do it, too.
Senior VPs and blah, blah, blah, blah.
Right?
I'm sure you can guess what it was related to.
And I am officially quitting that job on national TV and my boss is finding out right at the same time that you are.
So, you might say that I've got a little skin in this game.
[laughter] [cheering] That's right.
[applause] So, I'm gonna learn this stuff so that five years from now,
or three years from now, or however long it takes, when the systems are scalable enough to handle the Human Genome Project
because they are.
I mean, the thing practically fits in your pocket.
And all of the other hard problems that we can solve with data mining, I will be ready.
And I hope you guys are there with me.
So, have a great conference and thank you.
